paragraphs: He did find his father still at the table. The house had a dining room, but the table was laid, as usual, in the drawing room. That was the largest room, and it was furnished with an old-fashioned showiness. The furniture was white and very old, covered in worn red silky cloth. Between the windows hung mirrors in elaborate white and gilt frames, carved in the old style. The walls were papered in white, and the paper was torn in many places. Two large portraits hung there: one of some prince who had governed the district thirty years earlier, and one of some bishop, also long dead. In the corner opposite the door stood several ikons. A lamp was lit before them at nightfall ... less out of devotion than to light the room. Fyodor Pavlovitch went to bed very late, at three or four in the morning. Until then he would wander about the room at night, or sit in an armchair and think. It had become a habit. He often slept in the house quite alone, sending his servants off to the lodge. Usually, though, Smerdyakov stayed, sleeping on a bench in the hall.

When Alyosha came in, dinner was over, but coffee and preserves had been served. Fyodor Pavlovitch liked sweet things with his brandy after dinner. Ivan was at the table too, sipping coffee. The servants, Grigory and Smerdyakov, stood nearby. The gentlemen and the servants alike seemed to be in unusually good spirits. Fyodor Pavlovitch was roaring with laughter. Before Alyosha even entered the room, he heard that shrill laugh he knew so well. From the sound of it he could tell that his father had only reached the good-humored stage and was far from properly drunk.

“Here he is! Here he is!” yelled Fyodor Pavlovitch, delighted to see Alyosha. “Join us. Sit down. Coffee is a lenten dish, but it’s hot and good. I won’t offer you brandy, you’re keeping the fast. But would you like some? No, I’d better give you some of our famous liqueur. Smerdyakov, go to the cupboard, second shelf on the right. Here are the keys. Look sharp!”
Alyosha began to refuse the liqueur.
“Never mind. If you won’t have it, we will,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, beaming. “But wait—have you dined?”
“Yes,” answered Alyosha, who had in fact eaten only a piece of bread and drunk a glass of kvas in the Father Superior’s kitchen. “But I’d be glad of some hot coffee.”

“Bravo, my darling! He’ll have some coffee. Does it need warming? No, it’s boiling. It’s capital coffee: Smerdyakov made it. My Smerdyakov’s an artist with coffee, and with fish patties, and fish soup too. You must come one day and have some fish soup. Let me know beforehand.... But wait; didn’t I tell you this morning to come home with your mattress and pillow and all? Have you brought your mattress? He he he!”
“No, I haven’t,” said Alyosha, smiling too.

“Ah, but you were frightened, you were frightened this morning, weren’t you? There, my darling, I couldn’t do anything to upset you. Do you know, Ivan, I can’t resist the way he looks you straight in the face and laughs? It makes me laugh all over. I’m so fond of him. Alyosha, let me give you my blessing—a father’s blessing.”
Alyosha rose, but Fyodor Pavlovitch had already changed his mind.

“No, no,” he said. “I’ll just make the sign of the cross over you, for now. Sit still. Now we’ve got a treat for you, in your own line, too. It’ll make you laugh. Balaam’s ass has started talking to us here—and how he talks! How he talks!”

Balaam’s ass, it turned out, was the valet, Smerdyakov. He was a young man of about twenty-four, remarkably unsociable and silent. It wasn’t that he was shy or bashful. On the contrary, he was conceited and seemed to despise everybody.

But I must stop here and say a few words about him. He was brought up by Grigory and Marfa, but the boy grew up “with no sense of gratitude,” as Grigory put it. He was an unfriendly boy and seemed to look at the world with distrust. As a small child he was very fond of hanging cats and burying them with great ceremony. He would dress up in a sheet as if it were a surplice, and sing, and wave some object over the dead cat as if it were a censer. He did all this on the sly, in the greatest secrecy. Grigory caught him at this game once and gave him a sound beating. The boy shrank into a corner and sulked there for a week. “He doesn’t care for you or me, the monster,” Grigory used to say to Marfa, “and he doesn’t care for anyone. Are you a human being?” he said, speaking straight to the boy. “You’re not a human being. You grew out of the mildew in the bath-house.[2] That’s what you are.” Smerdyakov, as it turned out later, could never forgive him those words. Grigory taught him to read and write, and when the boy was twelve he began teaching him the Scriptures. But this teaching came to nothing. At the second or third lesson the boy suddenly grinned.
“What are you grinning at?” asked Grigory, looking at him threateningly from under his spectacles.
“Oh, nothing. God created light on the first day, and the sun, moon and stars on the fourth day. Where did the light come from on the first day?”

Grigory was thunderstruck. The boy looked at his teacher with a sneer. There was even something condescending in his expression. Grigory could not control himself. “I’ll show you where!” he cried, and gave the boy a violent slap on the cheek. The boy took the slap without a word, but withdrew into his corner again for some days. A week later he had his first attack of the disease he suffered from for the rest of his life—epilepsy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard of it, his attitude to the boy seemed to change at once. Until then he had taken no notice of him, though he never scolded him, and always gave him a kopeck when he met him. Sometimes, when he was in a good mood, he would send the boy something sweet from his table. But as soon as he heard of the illness, he took an active interest in him. He sent for a doctor and tried remedies, but the disease turned out to be incurable. The fits came, on average, once a month, but at irregular intervals. They also varied in violence: some were light and some were very severe. Fyodor Pavlovitch strictly forbade Grigory to use corporal punishment on the boy, and began letting him come upstairs to see him. He also forbade anyone to teach him anything for the time being. One day, when the boy was about fifteen, Fyodor Pavlovitch noticed him lingering by the bookcase, reading the titles through the glass. Fyodor Pavlovitch had a fair number of books—over a hundred—but no one ever saw him reading. He at once gave Smerdyakov the key to the bookcase. “Come, read. You shall be my librarian. You’ll be better off sitting and reading than hanging about the courtyard. Come, read this,” and Fyodor Pavlovitch gave him _Evenings in a Cottage near Dikanka_.
He read a little but didn’t like it. He didn’t smile once, and ended by frowning.
“Why? Isn’t it funny?” asked Fyodor Pavlovitch.
Smerdyakov did not speak.
“Answer, stupid!”
“It’s all untrue,” mumbled the boy, with a grin.
“Then go to the devil! You have the soul of a lackey. Wait, here’s Smaragdov’s _Universal History_. That’s all true. Read that.”
But Smerdyakov did not get through ten pages of Smaragdov. He found it dull. So the bookcase was closed again.

Soon afterwards Marfa and Grigory reported to Fyodor Pavlovitch that Smerdyakov was gradually becoming extraordinarily fussy. He would sit in front of his soup, pick up his spoon and look into the soup, bend over it, examine it, take a spoonful and hold it up to the light.
“What is it? A beetle?” Grigory would ask.
“A fly, maybe,” remarked Marfa.

The squeamish youth never answered, but he did the same with his bread, his meat, and everything else he ate. He would hold a piece on his fork up to the light, scrutinize it as if through a microscope, and only after long deliberation decide to put it in his mouth.
“Ach! What fine gentleman’s airs!” Grigory muttered, watching him.

When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard of this development in Smerdyakov, he decided to make him his cook, and sent him to Moscow to be trained. He spent some years there and came back remarkably changed in appearance. He looked extraordinarily old for his age. His face had become wrinkled and yellow, and strangely like a eunuch’s. In character he seemed almost exactly the same as before he left. He was just as unsociable, and showed not the slightest wish for anyone’s company. In Moscow, too, as we heard afterwards, he had always been silent. Moscow itself had little interest for him; he saw very little there and hardly took notice of anything. He went to the theater once, but came back silent and displeased with it. On the other hand, he returned to us from Moscow well dressed, in a clean coat and clean linen. Twice a day, without fail, he brushed his clothes with great care, and he was very fond of cleaning his smart calf boots with a special English polish, so that they shone like mirrors. He turned out to be a first-rate cook. Fyodor Pavlovitch paid him a salary, and Smerdyakov spent almost all of it on clothes, pomade, perfumes and the like. But he seemed to have as much contempt for women as for men; he was discreet with them, almost unapproachable. Fyodor Pavlovitch began to look on him rather differently. His fits were becoming more frequent, and on the days he was ill Marfa did the cooking, which did not suit Fyodor Pavlovitch at all.
“Why are your fits getting worse?” asked Fyodor Pavlovitch, looking sideways at his new cook. “Would you like to get married? Shall I find you a wife?”

But Smerdyakov turned pale with anger and made no reply. Fyodor Pavlovitch left him with an impatient gesture. The main thing was that he trusted his honesty completely. Once, when Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk, he dropped three hundred-rouble notes in the muddy courtyard, notes he had only just received. He didn’t miss them until the next day, and was just hurrying to search his pockets when he saw the notes lying on the table. Where had they come from? Smerdyakov had picked them up and brought them in the day before.

“Well, my lad, I’ve never met anyone like you,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said curtly, and gave him ten roubles. I should add that he not only believed in his honesty but, for some reason, even liked him, although the young man looked at him as sullenly as at everyone else, and was always silent. He rarely spoke. If anyone at the time had wondered what interested the young man and what was in his mind, it would have been impossible to tell by looking at him. Yet he would sometimes stop suddenly in the house, or even in the yard or the street, and stand still for ten minutes, lost in thought. A student of faces, studying his, would have said that there was no thought in it, no reflection, only a sort of contemplation. There is a remarkable picture by the painter Kramskoy called “Contemplation.” It shows a forest in winter, and on a road through the forest, in complete solitude, stands a peasant in a torn kaftan and bark shoes. He stands as if lost in thought. Yet he is not thinking; he is “contemplating.” If anyone touched him, he would start and look at them as though waking up, bewildered. It’s true he would come to himself at once; but if he were asked what he had been thinking about, he would remember nothing. Yet probably he keeps hidden inside himself the impression that dominated him during that contemplation. Those impressions are dear to him, and no doubt he hoards them without noticing, even unconsciously. How and why, of course, he does not know either. He may suddenly, after hoarding impressions for many years, give up everything and go off to Jerusalem on a pilgrimage for the salvation of his soul, or perhaps he will suddenly set fire to his native village, or perhaps do both. There are a good many “contemplatives” among the peasantry. Well, Smerdyakov was probably one of them, and he was probably greedily hoarding up his impressions, hardly knowing why.
